Calculate English readability with visible counting decisions

Source: vignettes/english-readability.Rmd
english-readability.Rmd

How much of a readability difference comes from sentence length, and how much from counting syllables? Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level combine these components. Keeping the counts beside the score lets you inspect the result before interpreting a difference between texts.

This guide uses ldfreq 0.3.0.9012 or later. The helpers in examples/readability.R are explicitly sourced installed examples, not exported functions. They calculate the published formulas under recorded counting conditions. Automatic syllables use optional nsyllable >= 1.0.1 and are estimates; hand-supplied counts need no optional package. These examples do not establish accuracy on learner writing or validate a reader’s ability, a school placement, or an L2 proficiency level. Only declared English input is supported.

Start from sentences and inspect what was counted 

library(ldfreq)

demo <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "readability-demo.R",
  package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), demo)
helper <- demo$helper
prepared <- demo$prepared
analysis <- demo$analysis
print(prepared$segments[c("document_id", "segment_id", "text", "status")], row.names = FALSE)
#>  document_id segment_id                  text           status
#>           d1         s1          The cat sat.          counted
#>           d1         s2          The dog ran.          counted
#>           d1    heading A heading to exclude. excluded_segment
#>           d2         s1 A little rabbit runs.          counted
#>           d3         s1 In 1918, R.F.D. grew.          counted
#>           d4         s1                               no_words
#>           d5         s1                 Bird.          counted

These short, authored texts expose the arithmetic; they are not a readability validation sample. Supply one sentence per segment, with unique document_id/segment_id pairs and the original text. An empty document still has a row with text = "". Preserve the original file and the boundary decisions used to produce these segments. Offsets in the result are local to each supplied segment, not offsets into an unsupplied file.

helper <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "readability.R", package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), helper)
prepared <- helper$readability_prepare(segments, language = "en",
  sentence_policy = "reviewed sentence boundaries; headings excluded",
  include = include_sentence)

sentence_policy describes your procedure; it does not run a sentence splitter. The helper counts each included segment containing at least one word as one sentence. It does not silently filter out very short or long sentences. Review abbreviations, fragments, quotations, lists, colons and semicolons when defining boundaries. Kincaid and colleagues’ original instructions, pp. 39–40 include independent units and fragments; punctuation alone is not a complete boundary rule. language = "en" is your declaration, not automatic detection.

The English tokenizer retains contractions, hyphenated words, dotted initialisms and numeric expressions. URLs, email addresses and punctuation are excluded. Original text and token spans remain available, including excluded sentences and the tokenizer’s URL/email audit. Curly apostrophes and two Unicode hyphens have canonical token surfaces; their original surfaces and code-point positions are also saved. No Unicode normalization or case folding is applied at this stage.

These are operational word rules, not a reproduction of every original sampling and counting instruction. For example, a standalone currency symbol does not become a spoken word in this tokenizer. Flesch’s 1948 instructions, reprinted on pp. 106–107 count hyphenated forms as one word and syllables by pronunciation, including figures and symbols. They also describe 100-word sampling with a sentence-end adjustment. Here the ratios use all included text. Audit mismatches before use; if the operational word units do not fit your protocol, this helper is unsuitable for that protocol. Do not force its word total to equal a lexical-diversity analysis with different preprocessing.

Estimate syllables, then review pronunciations 

automatic <- helper$readability_score(prepared)
audit <- cbind(prepared$tokens[c("document_id", "segment_id", "original_surface", "counted")],
  automatic$syllables[c("syllables", "method")])
print(audit, row.names = FALSE)

nsyllable uses a pronunciation dictionary and a vowel-group fallback for unknown words. The helper distinguishes dictionary matches, fallback estimates and unavailable counts. A finite estimate is not a verified pronunciation. Digits and dotted initialisms are withheld for explicit pronunciation review, even if a vowel guess would return a number. Other abbreviations, names, compounds, misspellings and pronunciation variants also require review. The result records the package version, dictionary hash, lowercase policy and estimation method.

Every included word contributes to the word denominator. If even one lacks a syllable count, both formula scores are NA; the known syllable subtotal and number of unresolved words remain visible. Missing counts are not replaced by one, and unresolved words are not removed from the denominator.

In the hand-counted example, 1918 and R.F.D. initially have no pronunciation decision. The second analysis supplies four and three syllables respectively, with the spoken forms recorded in review_reason.

print(demo$initial$components, row.names = FALSE)
#>  document_id words sentences syllables known_syllables missing_syllable_words
#>           d1     6         2         6               6                      0
#>           d2     4         1         6               6                      0
#>           d3     4         1        NA               2                      2
#>           d4     0         0        NA               0                      0
#>           d5     1         1         1               1                      0
#>  below_word_threshold            status
#>                  TRUE                ok
#>                  TRUE                ok
#>                  TRUE missing_syllables
#>                  TRUE          no_words
#>                  TRUE                ok
print(subset(demo$reviewed, nzchar(review_reason),
  select = c(token_row, syllables, method, review_reason)), row.names = FALSE)
#>  token_row syllables                 method
#>         16         4 declared pronunciation
#>         17         3 declared pronunciation
#>                                   review_reason
#>                  nineteen eighteen: 4 syllables
#>  letters R, F, D spoken separately: 3 syllables

For your own review, copy the complete syllable table, edit its counts and methods, and retain reasons alongside the unchanged first analysis. The source_id and token_row keys bind counts to this preparation; tables from a different source or sentence policy, duplicate keys and missing rows fail. Rows can be reordered because the keys determine alignment. All source tokens, including excluded sentences, keep a row; their unresolved counts do not make included text unavailable.

reviewed <- automatic$syllables
reviewed$review_reason <- ""
# Change selected syllables, method, and review_reason after inspecting the text.
analysis <- helper$readability_score(prepared, reviewed,
  syllable_source = "pronunciation review; decisions recorded in review_reason")
record <- list(automatic = automatic, analysis = analysis, session = sessionInfo())

To supply counts entirely by hand, construct the same four columns: source_id (the preparation’s integrity_sha256), token_row, syllables, and method. Counts are positive whole numbers or NA, never zero. A descriptive syllable_source is required. Extra review columns are retained. The executable readability-demo.R shows this without requiring nsyllable.

Check components before interpreting scores

Let W be counted words, S counted sentences and Sy the complete syllable total.

Measure Formula
Flesch Reading Ease 206.835 − 1.015 W/S − 84.6 Sy/W
Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level 0.39 W/S + 11.8 Sy/W − 15.59

The first is Flesch’s reading-ease equation. The second is the recalibrated equation in Kincaid et al. (1975), p. 40. That recalibration used Navy personnel and training-manual passages; its study description does not establish a universal grade interpretation for L2 writers or readers.

print(analysis$results[c("document_id", "measure", "value", "words", "sentences",
  "syllables", "below_word_threshold", "status")], digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
#>  document_id              measure  value words sentences syllables
#>           d1  Flesch_Reading_Ease 119.19     6         2         6
#>           d1 Flesch_Kincaid_Grade  -2.62     6         2         6
#>           d2  Flesch_Reading_Ease  75.88     4         1         6
#>           d2 Flesch_Kincaid_Grade   3.67     4         1         6
#>           d3  Flesch_Reading_Ease  12.43     4         1         9
#>           d3 Flesch_Kincaid_Grade  12.52     4         1         9
#>           d4  Flesch_Reading_Ease     NA     0         0        NA
#>           d4 Flesch_Kincaid_Grade     NA     0         0        NA
#>           d5  Flesch_Reading_Ease 121.22     1         1         1
#>           d5 Flesch_Kincaid_Grade  -3.40     1         1         1
#>  below_word_threshold   status
#>                  TRUE       ok
#>                  TRUE       ok
#>                  TRUE       ok
#>                  TRUE       ok
#>                  TRUE       ok
#>                  TRUE       ok
#>                  TRUE no_words
#>                  TRUE no_words
#>                  TRUE       ok
#>                  TRUE       ok

For d1, the two three-word sentences contain six syllables: W = 6, S = 2, Sy = 6. Reading Ease is 119.190, and Grade Level is −2.620. Values are not clipped to 0–100 or to nonnegative grades. Neither these values nor a short text’s computable score implies meaningful precision or a reader classification.

below_word_threshold defaults to W < 100. This is a configurable advisory flag, not a validated minimum, exclusion rule, or reason to hide a score. Record your study’s sample-length policy separately. Zero words produce no_words and NA scores; no artificial sentence or syllable is added. Document scores use ratios of total counts, not averages of sentence scores.

quanteda.textstats implements both formulas. With identical component counts, the equations agree. Its defaults can produce different inputs: hyphens may be split, sentence length filters apply, and unavailable syllable estimates are replaced by one in its implementation. This helper reuses the optional syllable estimator but exposes missingness and your supplied boundaries. Agreement on ordinary examples does not establish end-to-end equivalence for arbitrary texts.

Keep writer, task and occasion in the research table 

print(demo$study_long[c("observation_id", "writer_id", "task", "occasion",
  "document_id", "measure", "value", "words", "status")], digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
#>  observation_id writer_id        task occasion document_id              measure
#>              o1        w1 description       t1          d1 Flesch_Kincaid_Grade
#>              o1        w1 description       t1          d1  Flesch_Reading_Ease
#>              o2        w1   narrative       t2          d2 Flesch_Kincaid_Grade
#>              o2        w1   narrative       t2          d2  Flesch_Reading_Ease
#>              o3        w2 description       t1          d3 Flesch_Kincaid_Grade
#>              o3        w2 description       t1          d3  Flesch_Reading_Ease
#>              o4        w2   narrative       t2          d4 Flesch_Kincaid_Grade
#>              o4        w2   narrative       t2          d4  Flesch_Reading_Ease
#>              o5        w3 description       t1          d5 Flesch_Kincaid_Grade
#>              o5        w3 description       t1          d5  Flesch_Reading_Ease
#>              o6        w3   narrative       t2        <NA> Flesch_Kincaid_Grade
#>              o6        w3   narrative       t2        <NA>  Flesch_Reading_Ease
#>   value words        status
#>   -2.62     6            ok
#>  119.19     6            ok
#>    3.67     4            ok
#>   75.88     4            ok
#>   12.52     4            ok
#>   12.43     4            ok
#>      NA     0      no_words
#>      NA     0      no_words
#>   -3.40     1            ok
#>  121.22     1            ok
#>      NA    NA not_submitted
#>      NA    NA not_submitted

The executable example joins a planned observation roster and a unique observation/document mapping to the two measures by document ID. The sixth observation was not submitted; its word count stays NA. The submitted empty fourth document has zero words. These states remain distinct, as do unresolved syllables in the first analysis. analysis_id identifies the saved input, syllable decisions and settings. Keep one row per observation and selected measure in a model; do not stack both differently scaled scores as replications.

model_data <- subset(demo$study_long,
  measure == "Flesch_Reading_Ease" & status == "ok")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(model_data$observation_id),
  length(unique(model_data$analysis_id)) == 1L)

This is an ordinary data frame with writer, task and occasion available to lme4. A hypothetical formula is shown below; the tiny authored dataset is insufficient to justify fitting it. Specify predictors, coding, random effects and sample-length exclusions from your research design. The repeated-observations guide demonstrates an actual model workflow and its diagnostics. This readability table is separate from the lexical-metric plan contract used there.

fit <- lme4::lmer(value ~ task + occasion + (1 | writer_id), data = model_data)

Save enough to return to the text

Choose a lasting private path for the RDS and CSV; relative paths start at getwd(). The following uses the current directory.

saveRDS(demo$record, "readability-record.rds", version = 2)
write.csv(demo$study_long, "readability-study-long.csv", row.names = FALSE, na = "NA")
saved <- readRDS("readability-record.rds")
helper$readability_validate(saved$analysis)
saved$analysis$source$segments
saved$analysis$source$tokens
saved$analysis$syllables

In a fresh R session, use the same package snapshot and your saved path. No automatic syllable counter is needed to inspect the retained counts:

library(ldfreq)
helper <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "readability.R", package = "ldfreq",
  mustWork = TRUE), helper)
saved <- readRDS("readability-record.rds")
helper$readability_validate(saved$analysis)
saved$analysis$source$segments
saved$analysis$syllables
saved$study_long

The full record retains both analyses, original segments, tokenization audits, source offsets, counts, decisions, formulas and session information. The hash check detects changed saved fields; it is not a judgment that the original sentence or pronunciation decisions were correct. Pin the package revision and keep the full RDS alongside the CSV. The flat table alone cannot recover the counting decisions.
